939.title: Azusa Street (1906)
939.hook: a Black preacher, William Seymour, leads a revival in a plain Los Angeles mission building where races worship together
939.howItsDone: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians often worship with spontaneous singing, raised hands, prayer for healing and prayer in tongues, and some churches remember Azusa Street as one of their beginnings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charles de Foucauld, the soldier who became a hermit in the Sahara. Your line was universal brother. Whose name did you learn, or whose answer did you wait for? Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

Sawdust on the floor. Planks laid across boxes for benches. A shabby old building on a side street in Los Angeles that had been used for storage and, by some accounts, as a stable. The preacher at the front is a Black man named William Seymour, the son of formerly enslaved parents, blind in one eye. Sometimes he prays with his head inside an empty wooden crate. And the room is packed. Black washerwomen, white laborers, Mexican families, newcomers from all over, kneeling side by side, in a country where race usually kept people apart. Newspapers mocked it. People kept coming. Today, the building and the name of its street.
screen: `A PREACHER WITH HIS HEAD IN A CRATE.`

segments.voice: What the people at Azusa Street said they were living through was the Book of Acts, happening again. On the day of Pentecost, Acts says, the first followers of Jesus were gathered in one place, and in the King James Bible: "they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." At Azusa Street, people prayed aloud in tongues, sang without hymnbooks, wept, shouted, fell quiet, and prayed for the sick. The meetings went on day after day. Pentecostal churches tell Azusa Street as one of their beginnings, and so do some charismatic Christians in other churches. Here, Christians differ, and it's worth saying plainly who says what. Pentecostals hold that the gifts in Acts, tongues and healing among them, are for today. Some other Christians believe those gifts belonged mainly to the apostles' time, and worship in quieter ways. Both read the same Bible. Now the part that gives today its line. A white participant named Frank Bartleman wrote afterward that at Azusa Street, the color line was washed away in the blood, meaning the blood of Christ. In a country where race divided churches and much else, a Black preacher led, and people of every color prayed for each other. Paul had written it long before: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." Honesty matters here too. The unity didn't last everywhere. In the years after, some churches that grew out of the revival split along the same color line again. That's part of the story. So is the room where, for a while, it was washed away.

Here's the practice: worship, or simply gather, with people different from you. Today, start by noticing. Settle, and breathe. Picture the last place you prayed, sang, or sat in silence with others. Who was in the room? Who looked like you, and who didn't? Don't judge it. Just see it. Then think of one place nearby where people unlike you gather: a church across town, a service in another language, a community meal. If you pray, you can pray for that room. If you don't, hold it in mind, and consider walking in one day. The bell holds the time.
Azusa Street. A side street in Los Angeles where a Black preacher led a revival, and people of every color knelt together.
Your line: the color line washed away. Today, notice one line in your own week that sorts people, a table, a group chat, a pew, and cross it once. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

940.title: Pandita Ramabai
940.hook: an Indian scholar and reformer who founded a home for widows and translated the Bible into Marathi
940.howItsDone: The community Ramabai founded near Pune still cares for women and children, and Marathi-speaking Christians remember her as a translator of their Bible.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Azusa Street, the revival where people of every color knelt together. Your line was the color line washed away. Which line did you cross, even once? Day nine hundred forty.

A young woman stands before a hall of learned men in Calcutta and recites Sanskrit verse from memory, long passages of it, and answers their questions. They're so impressed they give her titles of honor, and one of them sticks to her name for the rest of her life: Pandita, a learned woman. Her father had taught her Sanskrit himself, a gift not every girl of her time was given. She has walked across much of India with her family. She will soon be married, then widowed, with a baby daughter in her arms. And what she builds next will be a door for women with nowhere else to go.

In the India Ramabai grew up in, a widow's life could be very hard. Some were only girls when their husbands died. Custom in some families could mean a shaved head, plain clothes, no remarriage, no schooling, and a life spent at the back of the house. Hindu reformers of her day were working to change this too. Ramabai knew it from the inside. After her own husband's death she traveled to England, and there, among Anglican sisters, she was baptized. She kept asking questions the whole way, and didn't take everything she was told on trust. She went on to America, where she lectured and raised support. Then she came home and did something practical. She opened a home for widows, a place where they could live safely and, just as important, learn. Later she built a larger community on farmland outside Pune and called it Mukti, a word for freedom or deliverance. Women and girls who had been turned away found beds, classrooms, work and dignity there. Her reason was in the Bible she now read. The Letter of James puts it bluntly, in the King James Bible: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction." Not only feel for them. Visit them. Ramabai went further and gave them a home. And she did one more thing, the work of her later years. She translated the whole Bible into Marathi, her people's everyday language, working from the Hebrew and Greek herself. A scholar who had once recited Sanskrit to learned men spent her last years making sure the women of her own region could read scripture in the words they spoke at home.

Here's the practice: support a woman's education, starting with one name. Settle, and breathe. Think of a woman who taught you something: a teacher, a grandmother, an aunt, a coworker who showed you the ropes. Then think of the women and girls today who are still kept from school, by money, by custom, or by war. You don't have to fix it in two minutes. Just pick one step you could take this week: a book given, a school fund, a word of encouragement to a girl who's studying. If you pray, you can pray for her. The bell holds the time.
Pandita Ramabai. A Sanskrit scholar from India who became a Christian, opened a home for widows, and translated the Bible into Marathi.
Your line: a home for widows. Today, find one person living alone after a loss, and visit, call, or send a message that asks for nothing back. Day nine hundred forty.

941.title: Sadhu Sundar Singh
941.hook: a Sikh-born Indian who became a wandering Christian holy man in saffron robes
941.howItsDone: Christians in South Asia worship in many styles, and some use Indian forms such as sitting on the floor, bhajan-style songs and saffron dress for those who live as wandering preachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pandita Ramabai, the scholar who opened a home for widows and translated the Bible into Marathi. Your line was a home for widows. Who did you visit or call? Day nine hundred forty-one.

A traveler on a hot day in India collapses on a railway platform. Someone runs to fetch water and comes back with it in a cup that belongs to the railway. The man on the ground, half fainting, refuses to drink. Not because he isn't thirsty. Because of the cup. Then someone brings the same water in his own brass vessel, and he drinks it gladly. A wandering holy man in a saffron robe told that story, and he used it to say something about the gospel and India. His name is today's word.

Sundar Singh grew up in a Sikh family in the Punjab. His mother, by his own telling, took him to hear holy men and to read sacred writings, and he loved her deeply. When she died, he was young, and in his grief he grew angry at everything, including the Christian missionaries' book, which by his own account he tore and burned. Then, his story goes, he prayed through a night asking God to show himself, and before dawn he saw Jesus. He became a Christian. His family could not accept it, and he left home. What he did next is the heart of today. India already had a figure everyone recognized: the sadhu, the wandering holy man with no possessions, walking from village to village in a saffron robe. Sundar Singh put on that robe. He walked barefoot, slept where he was offered a place, and told stories about Jesus in the languages of the villages he passed through. He went over the mountain passes into Tibet to preach, and on his last journey there he never came back. Nobody knows what happened to him. The railway story was his answer to a question. Why does the gospel sometimes sound foreign in India? Because, he said, it had been handed over in a European cup. The water was what people needed. Jesus told a woman at a well, in the King James Bible: "But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst." Water, Sundar Singh said, can come in an Indian cup. Christians still disagree about how much of a culture the gospel should wear. Sundar Singh's answer was a saffron robe and bare feet.

Here's the practice: pray, or be still, in the way that fits you. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself what shape stillness takes in your life. Maybe it's a song from your grandmother's kitchen. A language you only speak at home. Sitting cross-legged, or kneeling, or walking. Notice whether you've ever borrowed someone else's cup because you thought it was the proper one. For these two minutes, use your own. If you pray, pray in the words and posture that feel like home. If you don't, sit in the way your body knows best. The bell holds the time.
Sadhu Sundar Singh. A man raised in a Sikh family in the Punjab who followed Jesus as a wandering holy man in a saffron robe.
Your line: water in an Indian cup. Today, when you share something you care about, pour it into the other person's cup: their words, their way, their world. Day nine hundred forty-one.

942.title: The prophet Harris
942.hook: a Liberian evangelist walks West Africa in a white robe, and tradition says crowds are baptized
942.howItsDone: Members of the Harrist Church in Côte d'Ivoire, and some Methodists in the region, remember William Wadé Harris as the preacher who first brought the gospel to their villages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sadhu Sundar Singh and his story of the railway cup. Your line was water in an Indian cup. Whose cup did you pour into? Day nine hundred forty-two.

A prison cell in Liberia. The man inside is a schoolteacher and church worker named William Wadé Harris, locked up for his part in a political protest. By his own account, while he's there, an angel comes to him in a vision and tells him to put away his European clothes, dress simply, and go out as a preacher. When he walks out of prison, he does exactly that. He has a long white gown, a tall staff with a cross on top, a Bible, and a gourd rattle to call people together. No mission board sent him. No salary is waiting. He sets off along the coast on foot. Today, the walk.
screen: `A WHITE GOWN, A CROSS-STAFF, A BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Harris walked east, out of Liberia and along the coast of what is now Côte d'Ivoire and into what is now Ghana. Village to village, on foot. He preached in simple words, prayed for the sick, and baptized people who wanted to follow Jesus. Tradition says the crowds grew so large that colonial officials grew nervous and finally sent him back home. His time on the road was short. Then comes the surprising part. Harris didn't try to build his own organization. He told the new believers to build simple prayer houses, to keep Sunday, and to wait. Teachers with the Bible would come, he said, and they should listen to them. Then he walked on. Years later, missionaries arriving in some of those villages found congregations already gathered, keeping Sunday, singing, and waiting for someone to teach them. Some of those believers joined the Methodist church. Others kept his name and founded the Harrist Church, which continues today. Christians disagree about how to describe Harris. Some call him an evangelist, some a prophet, some a forerunner of the independent African churches. He called himself a prophet. Isaiah has a line about people like him, in the King James Bible: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace." Notice it praises the feet. Not the voice, not the robe. The feet. Harris preached with his walking. Every village heard him because he had walked there.

Here's the practice: walk and pray, or walk and pay attention. If you can, stand up now and walk slowly, in a room, a hallway, or outside. Feel each step land. Heel, then toe. If you can't walk, let each breath be a step. With each step, name one person or place you'll pass today. The office. The bus driver. A neighbor's door. If you pray, you can hold each one before God as you step. If you don't, simply carry them with you, one step at a time. The bell holds the time.
The prophet Harris. A Liberian preacher who walked the West African coast in a white gown with a cross-staff, and told new believers to wait for teachers with the Bible.
Your line: the walking prophet. Today, take one walk on purpose, even ten minutes, and let your feet do the praying or the noticing. Day nine hundred forty-two.

943.title: Simon Kimbangu
943.hook: a Congolese healer spends the rest of his life in prison, and a church grows from it
943.howItsDone: Kimbanguists gather at Nkamba, which they call a holy place, to pray and sing, and they honor Simon Kimbangu as a prophet who suffered for the gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prophet Harris, who walked the West African coast and told people to wait for teachers. Your line was the walking prophet. Where did your feet take you? Day nine hundred forty-three.

Nkamba is a village in the lower Congo, in the hills. One day, the story goes, a Baptist catechist named Simon Kimbangu lays his hands on a sick woman and prays, and she gets up. Word spreads. Soon paths into the village are worn down by people carrying the sick on their backs and on stretchers. Markets empty. Some workers walk off their jobs to go and hear him. The Belgian colonial officials who run the Congo don't like any of it. A crowd that big, following a Congolese man, looks to them like trouble. Today, what they did, and what grew anyway.

Kimbangu's public ministry was short. He preached from the Bible, prayed for the sick, told people to turn from violence and to put away old objects of spiritual power, and called them to follow Jesus. The authorities ordered his arrest. For a while he stayed out of their reach. Then, tradition says, he gave himself up, and told his followers not to fight for him. There's an echo of that night in Gethsemane, when Jesus said to the disciple who drew a sword, in the King James Bible: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." A colonial court sentenced him to death. The sentence was changed to life in prison, and he was taken far from home, to a prison at the other end of the country. He never came home. He died there. Here's the strange part of the story. The man was locked away, his followers were watched, and some were exiled to distant parts of the colony. And the movement didn't vanish. It spread. Exiled families carried his teaching wherever they were sent. Out of that grew a church, the Church of Jesus Christ on Earth through the Prophet Simon Kimbangu, which Kimbanguists say grew from his suffering. Its members honor him as God's prophet. Other churches describe him in their own ways, and some differ with Kimbanguists about his place. The Letter to the Hebrews asks Christians to remember people in prison, in the King James words, "as bound with them". For Kimbanguists, the prison is not where the story ended. It's where the church began.

Here's the practice: pray for Congo, or hold it in mind. Settle, and breathe. Congo is a huge country of rivers, forests and cities, of families, churches, mosques and markets, and it has known a great deal of suffering. You don't need to know all of it. Picture one family there this evening: a meal being cooked, children doing homework, someone worried about tomorrow. If you pray, you can name Congo before God and ask for peace for that family. If you don't, let your attention rest on them, the way you'd hold a friend's name. The bell holds the time.
Simon Kimbangu. A Congolese catechist and healer who gave himself up, died in a colonial prison, and whose followers built a church.
Your line: a church from a prison. Today, when something you care about is shut away or cut short, look for what is still growing from it, and tend that. Day nine hundred forty-three.

944.title: The new martyrs of Russia
944.hook: after the Russian Revolution, priests, nuns and lay people are killed or sent to camps
944.howItsDone: The Russian Orthodox Church keeps a feast of the new martyrs and confessors of Russia, with icons that gather many of them together, and parishes pray for those who suffer for their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simon Kimbangu, who gave himself up and died in a colonial prison. Your line was a church from a prison. What did you find still growing? Day nine hundred forty-four.

Before the revolution, she was a princess. Elizabeth, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria, married into the Russian royal family. When a bomb killed her husband, she went to the prison and visited the man who had thrown it, and told him she forgave him. Then she gave away her jewels, put on a plain religious habit, and opened a convent in Moscow to nurse the poor. After the revolution, she was arrested. Tradition says that when her captors threw her and others down a mine shaft, people heard them singing hymns from below. She is one name in today's story.

After the Russian Revolution, the new Soviet state set out to push religion out of public life. Churches were closed, looted, turned into warehouses or blown up. Bishops, priests, monks and nuns were shot or sent to labor camps in the far north and east. So were ordinary parishioners: a church warden, a choir singer, a grandmother who hid icons. On the island of Solovki, an old monastery became a prison camp. The Orthodox Church calls these people the new martyrs and confessors of Russia. A martyr is someone who dies for the faith. A confessor is someone who suffers for it and lives. Here's the word inside the word. In the New Testament, before Jesus rises into heaven, he tells his followers, in the King James Bible: "ye shall be witnesses unto me." Later in the same King James Bible, the Greek word behind witness is put into English another way, in Revelation: "Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you." Witness and martyr, one word. A martyr is first of all a witness. What did these witnesses do? Accounts from the camps describe priests hearing confessions in whispers during work, Easter hymns sung under the breath in a barracks, bread saved to share with someone weaker. Not heroics for show. Faithfulness, in small hidden ways, where it could cost everything. The Book of Revelation has a line written to a suffering church: "be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life." The same years were hard for Catholics, Baptists, Jews, Muslims and Buddhists under that state too. The Orthodox Church now keeps a feast for its new martyrs, and reads their names.

Here's the practice: pray for the persecuted, or hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. People are still punished today, in different places and under different powers, for what they believe or how they worship. Some are Christians. Some follow other faiths, or none. Picture one person sitting in a cell tonight because of what they believe. You don't know their name. That's fine. Hold them anyway. If you pray, you can ask that they be kept faithful and kept safe. If you don't, let them be real to you for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The new martyrs of Russia. Orthodox Christians, clergy and lay people, who were killed or sent to camps under the Soviet state, and whom the Orthodox Church honors as witnesses.
screen: `THE NEW MARTYRS OF RUSSIA — today's word`.

945.title: The Christmas truce (1914)
945.hook: soldiers climb out of the trenches to sing carols and share food with the enemy
945.carry: silent night in no man's land
945.howItsDone: At Christmas, churches sing carols such as Silent Night, and some retell the Christmas truce in services that pray for peace between enemies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new martyrs of Russia, witnesses in the camps. Your line was faithful in the camps. What small hidden faithful thing did you do? Day nine hundred forty-five.

A cold, clear Christmas Eve in Flanders. Two lines of trenches, close enough to shout across. Between them, a strip of mud, wire and shell holes the soldiers call no man's land. Anyone who raises his head above the parapet risks a bullet. Then, on the German side, lights appear: small candles, and in places little Christmas trees set up along the trench. A voice starts singing, and others join. Stille Nacht. Silent night. On the British side, men listen. After a while, someone sings back. Today, what happened next.

Much of what we know comes from soldiers' letters home. In places along the line, men climbed out of their trenches, unarmed, and walked toward each other. They shook hands. They swapped what they had: chocolate, cigarettes, sausage, buttons from their uniforms, addresses to write to after the war. Some letters mention a kick-about with a ball. Both sides used the quiet to bury their dead, and in places they held services together over the graves. Then the truce ended, and the shooting started again. Honesty matters here. It didn't happen everywhere. In some sections, the shooting never stopped. Officers on both sides disapproved, and it was not repeated the same way. So why does it matter? Because of what the soldiers sang. The carols told a story both sides knew: the angels over the shepherds' fields, singing, in the King James Bible, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." Men who had been trying to kill each other found that they shared a song, a prayer and a holiday. Jesus once said, "Love your enemies." For a night, in a muddy field, some men did. This week, people kept stepping across something. Azusa Street, where the color line washed away. Pandita Ramabai, a home for widows. Sundar Singh, water in an Indian cup. Harris, the walking prophet. Kimbangu, a church from a prison. The martyrs, faithful in the camps. And now enemies sharing chocolate between the trenches.

Here's the practice: share something with an opponent. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you're on the other side of. A rival at work. A relative you argue with. Someone who votes the other way. Notice the trench you've both dug. Now picture a small truce: one thing you could hand across. A compliment you actually mean. A cup of coffee. A question asked out of real curiosity. You don't have to end the war. Just climb out for a moment. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
The Christmas truce. The night soldiers on opposite sides of the trenches sang carols, crossed no man's land, and shared what they had.
Your line: silent night in no man's land. Today, hand one small good thing across to someone you're at odds with, and see what they hand back. Day nine hundred forty-five.

what it means: in places along the front, enemies sang, shook hands, traded gifts and buried their dead together.
what a scholar hears: a truce known mostly from soldiers' letters, patchy along the line and not repeated, held together by carols both sides knew.
